slots.practicalActivity: Using decayProb = 1 - e^(-t/T1) with T1=100 microseconds, compute the decoherence probability for a 100ns gate and a 200ns gate by hand, confirming it roughly doubles as the lesson's Check Yourself asks. Then explain in writing why that near-linear relationship breaks down once gate durations start approaching T1 itself.
slots.deliverable: Your two hand-computed decoherence probabilities (100ns and 200ns) showing the near-doubling relationship, plus a written explanation of why the linear approximation fails as t approaches T1.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself precisely: if you measure a qubit in the computational basis before and after a Z error, you get identical statistics. Explain in writing how you could actually detect that a Z error happened -- what basis you'd need to measure in instead (the +/- basis) and why Z swaps |+> and |-> the same way X swaps |0> and |1>.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of how to detect an otherwise-invisible Z error by switching to the +/- measurement basis, with the X/Z symmetry argument stated explicitly.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the depolarizing channel's P(I), P(X), P(Y), P(Z) by hand for a new total error rate p=0.03 (not one of the lesson's three worked values), confirming P(I)=0.97 and P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=0.01 each. Then answer the Check Yourself: why might a threshold number computed from the symmetric depolarizing model still be a useful planning estimate for a real qubit with known Z-biased noise.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed depolarizing probabilities at p=0.03, plus a written explanation of why the symmetric model remains a useful planning tool even for biased real hardware.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with reasoning, not a guess: a team doubles T1 (halving decoherence error for a given gate duration) but changes nothing about pulse calibration, for a circuit previously dominated by gate error. Explain roughly how much total circuit error would improve, and what that tells the team about where to focus engineering effort instead.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why halving decoherence barely moves total error in a gate-error-dominated circuit, and what that implies about where the team should actually invest engineering effort.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's three-gate worked example by hand: compute each gate's combined error probability (decoherence + depolarizing - product), then compose all three survival probabilities to confirm the final ~0.57% total-error figure. Then answer the Check Yourself: extend the same method to 10 gates of similar durations/rates and determine whether total error stays below, around, or exceeds 2%.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-reproduced three-gate calculation matching the lesson's ~0.57% result, plus your own extended 10-gate estimate with reasoning for whether it crosses the 2% mark.

slots.practicalActivity: Using P(success) = sum of C(n,flips)*p^flips*(1-p)^(n-flips), compute the 3-bit and 5-bit repetition code success probabilities by hand for p=0.15 (a value not in the lesson's table), and answer the Check Yourself: can a larger code (n=5) ever have a worse success probability than a smaller one (n=3) at the same p, and why or why not based on the majority-vote failure condition.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed 3-bit and 5-bit success probabilities at p=0.15, plus a written answer explaining why larger n never underperforms smaller n at the same flip rate (for p below 0.5).

lessons.title: Why Classical Error Correction Doesn't Port Directly

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, in your own words, the three obstacles the lesson names (can't measure without disturbing, errors aren't just flip-or-not, can't copy via no-cloning) with one sentence each. Then answer the Check Yourself: explain why measuring a syndrome is exactly the mechanism that forces a continuous error into one of a few discrete outcomes, connecting it to measurement collapse.
slots.deliverable: Your three-item written list of the obstacles blocking a direct classical-to-quantum port, plus a written explanation of why syndrome measurement collapses a continuous error into a discrete one.

lessons.title: The No-Cloning Constraint on Quantum Error Correction

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself precisely: a friend says 'my quantum error-correcting code produces three copies of the input qubit to protect it.' Using the no-cloning theorem and the distinction between known-state preparation and cloning an unknown state, write up exactly what's wrong with that description, and what real codes do instead (spreading via entanglement, not copying).
slots.deliverable: A written correction of the friend's 'three copies' claim, explaining the no-cloning violation and describing entangled spreading as the real mechanism instead.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's own Check Yourself with real computation: a 7-bit repetition code has minimum distance 7. Using d >= 2t+1, solve for how many errors it can correct and how many it can detect, and confirm this matches the pattern you'd expect from the 3-bit (corrects 1, detects 2) and 5-bit (corrects 2, detects 4) codes.
slots.deliverable: Your worked solution for the 7-bit code's correction and detection power using d>=2t+1, with a written comparison confirming it extends the 3-bit/5-bit pattern consistently.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: using the verified syndrome table, work out what syndrome (Z1Z2, Z2Z3) you'd get if X errors hit BOTH qubit 1 and qubit 2 simultaneously starting from |000>, and determine whether the code's single-error correction procedure gets this double-error case right or wrong.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-worked syndrome computation for the simultaneous qubit-1-and-2 X error case, plus a written determination of whether the code's correction procedure succeeds or fails on this double error.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: if you applied BOTH an X error and a Z error to the same qubit in this code (a Y error), work out whether the bit-flip code's stabilizers would catch it, whether the phase-flip code's stabilizers would catch it, both, or neither -- reasoning from each code's known blind spot (bit-flip code blind to Z, phase-flip code blind to X).
slots.deliverable: A written determination of which stabilizer sets catch a combined X+Z (Y-type) error on a single qubit, reasoning explicitly from each code's known blind spot.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: the Shor code uses phase-flip code outer, bit-flip code inner. Work out in writing whether swapping that order (bit-flip outer, phase-flip inner) would still protect against an arbitrary single-qubit error, by tracing through what each layer is actually responsible for detecting in both orderings.
slots.deliverable: A written analysis of whether swapping the Shor code's outer/inner layer order still works, with explicit reasoning about what each layer detects in each configuration.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: suppose the ancilla measuring Z1Z2 itself suffers a measurement error and reports the wrong bit, even though no real X error occurred on the data qubits. Using the lesson 10 syndrome table, work out what incorrect 'correction' the decoder would apply, and what the resulting (now actually wrong) state would be.
slots.deliverable: A written trace of the incorrect correction a decoder would apply after a faulty ancilla readout, including the resulting (newly erroneous) physical state.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's Check Yourself trace by hand: starting from logical |0>_L = |000>, apply an X error to qubit 3, compute the Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 syndrome step by step, and confirm it matches the lesson 10 table's entry for errorPos=2 (syndrome 01, correction flips qubit 3).
slots.deliverable: Your complete hand trace (state after error, both stabilizer computations, syndrome, correction) for the |000> plus X-on-qubit-3 case, confirmed against the lesson 10 table.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: using the anticommutation rule, explain in writing why the bit-flip code's logical operator X_L = X1X2X3 commutes with both Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 (i.e. never triggers a syndrome) even though it changes the logical qubit's value -- work through the pairwise X/Z commutation on each shared qubit.
slots.deliverable: A written proof, using pairwise Pauli commutation on each shared qubit, that X1X2X3 commutes with both stabilizers while still acting non-trivially on the logical state.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: explain in writing why reusing the same 3 rows of H for both X-type and Z-type stabilizers (rather than needing 6 independent rows) depends specifically on H being self-orthogonal. Verify self-orthogonality yourself by computing the mod-2 dot product of row 1 with itself ([0,0,0,1,1,1,1] dotted with itself).
slots.deliverable: Your hand-verified mod-2 self-dot-product of row 1 (confirming it equals 0), plus a written explanation of why self-orthogonality is exactly what licenses reusing the same 3 rows for both stabilizer types.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: the lesson says C1 and C2 don't have to be the same classical code in general CSS constructions. Write out, precisely, what structural property two DIFFERENT classical codes C1 and C2 would need to satisfy (C2-perp subset of C1) for their CSS combination to produce valid, commuting stabilizers, and why that condition guarantees commutation.
slots.deliverable: A written statement of the nested-code condition (C2-perp subset of C1) required for two different codes to form a valid CSS code, with an explanation of why it guarantees stabilizer commutation.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: using column 1 of H = [0,0,1], work out what Z-type syndrome a Z error on qubit 1 would produce as an X-type error, and separately what an X error on qubit 1 would produce as a Z-type syndrome, using the column-lookup method demonstrated in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: Your two hand-computed syndromes (for a Z error and for an X error on qubit 1, both using column [0,0,1] of H) with the column-lookup reasoning shown explicitly.

lessons.title: Why the Surface Code Is the Leading Candidate

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: explain in writing why a code with an excellent theoretical minimum distance but a very low error threshold could be a worse practical choice than the surface code, even needing fewer physical qubits on paper. Then list the surface code's three named hardware-friendly properties (nearest-neighbor connectivity, favorable threshold, low-weight stabilizers) with one sentence each on why it matters.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why a low threshold can make an otherwise-efficient code impractical, plus your three-item list of the surface code's hardware-friendly properties with reasoning for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Using total = 2d^2 - 1, compute by hand the total physical qubits needed for a distance-19 surface code, confirming your own arithmetic. Then answer the Check Yourself: compare the absolute qubit increase from d=15 (449) to d=19 against the increase from d=3 (17) to d=7 (97), and state whether the increase is the same, larger, or smaller at higher distances, with the arithmetic shown.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed distance-19 total qubit count, plus a written comparison of the absolute qubit-count jumps at low versus high distance with the supporting arithmetic.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a single stabilizer's outcome flips in round 5 then reverts in round 6 with no correction applied in between. Using the lesson's distinction between a persistent defect (real error) and an isolated single-round flip (faulty measurement), determine which is the more likely explanation and write out your reasoning.
slots.deliverable: A written determination (faulty measurement, not real error) for the round-5-flip-then-round-6-revert scenario, with explicit reasoning tied to the persistent-vs-isolated-flip distinction.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why a decoder that is highly accurate but too slow to keep up with incoming syndrome rounds would still be a practical failure for running a real fault-tolerant computation, even though each individual decoding decision is correct. Name the specific consequence (backlog) explicitly.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why decoding speed, not just accuracy, determines practical usability, naming the backlog problem explicitly as the failure mode.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce Exercise 1 by hand: using total = 2d^2-1, data=d^2, ancilla=d^2-1, compute all three values for d=13 and d=17, confirming the lesson's 337 and 577 totals. Then answer the Check Yourself (Exercise 2's follow-up): if the same X error had instead occurred on an interior bulk qubit touched by 2 Z-type stabilizers instead of 1, how many defects would appear and why would that change the decoder's job.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-reproduced d=13 and d=17 qubit-count tables matching the lesson's 337 and 577 totals, plus a written answer on the two-defect bulk-qubit case and why it's harder for the decoder than the single-defect boundary case.

lessons.title: What a Logical Qubit Actually Costs in Physical Qubits
lessons.chapterTitle: Logical vs. Physical Qubits & Resource Estimation

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real numbers from the two tables: identify roughly at what physical-qubit budget concatenation's exponential cost (7^L) overtakes the surface code's quadratic cost (2d^2-1) for comparable protection, and explain in writing why that crossover point matters more than comparing the cheapest instance of each (surface d=3 vs concatenation L=1).
slots.deliverable: Your identified crossover point between the two cost tables with supporting numbers, plus a written explanation of why the crossover matters more than comparing the smallest instances.

lessons.title: The Error Threshold Theorem
lessons.chapterTitle: Logical vs. Physical Qubits & Resource Estimation

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real arithmetic: if p were exactly equal to p_th (p/p_th = 1), compute what (p/p_th)^((d+1)/2) equals for every value of d (it's always 1), and write out what that tells you about why operating exactly at threshold is still not good enough in practice -- no suppression occurs at any distance.
slots.deliverable: Your computed confirmation that (p/p_th)^exponent = 1 for all d when p=p_th, plus a written explanation of why operating exactly at threshold provides zero error suppression regardless of code distance.

lessons.title: Resource Estimation for a Real Algorithm
lessons.chapterTitle: Logical vs. Physical Qubits & Resource Estimation

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why a real detailed resource estimate for Shor's algorithm (like the cited Gidney & Ekera ~20-million-qubit figure) comes out different from simply multiplying 'physical qubits per logical qubit' by 'number of logical qubits,' naming magic-state distillation and real circuit structure as the missing overheads this lesson's simplified method doesn't capture.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation naming the specific overheads (magic-state distillation, real circuit structure) that make a literature-grade estimate differ from the lesson's simplified multiplication method.

lessons.title: Resource-Estimation Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Logical vs. Physical Qubits & Resource Estimation

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real computation: a third algorithm needs 200 logical qubits at distance 9 (161 physical qubits per logical qubit). Compute the total (200 x 161 = 32,200) by hand, then compare it against Scenario 1 (12,050) and Scenario 2 (29,140) from the lesson, and write up what the comparison tells you about the relative influence of logical-qubit count versus distance in this case.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed 32,200-qubit total for the 200-logical-qubit/distance-9 scenario, plus a written comparison against the lesson's two scenarios and what it reveals about count-versus-distance influence.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why a quantum computer using an excellent, high-distance error-correcting code, but implementing its syndrome-extraction circuits carelessly (without fault-tolerant gadget design), could still fail to be a fault-tolerant system overall -- naming the specific failure mode (a single faulty CNOT in the ancilla circuit spreading an error across multiple data qubits).
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of how careless syndrome-extraction circuitry can defeat an otherwise excellent code, naming the specific error-spreading failure mode.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why the Gottesman-Knill theorem means a fault-tolerant quantum computer built only from transversal Clifford gates, no matter how reliably it ran them, would still provide zero real quantum computational advantage. Then work out, for the 15-to-1 distillation protocol, how many noisy input magic states two full rounds of distillation would consume if each round's output feeds the next round's input (hint: 15 for the first high-fidelity state, then 15 more noisy copies needed to distill a second-round input, etc. -- reason through the multiplicative cost in your own words).
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why Clifford-only circuits provide no quantum advantage (citing Gottesman-Knill and classical simulability), plus a written reasoning-through of how distillation's multiplicative cost compounds across repeated rounds.

lessons.title: The Current State of Fault-Tolerant Hardware

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why 'a logical qubit's error rate was shown lower than its best physical qubit's error rate' counts as a genuine, important milestone, while still being far short of fault-tolerant computing at a useful scale. Name the specific categorical gap (small number of logical qubits demonstrated vs. the hundreds-to-millions a real algorithm needs, per chapter 6's own math).
slots.deliverable: A written explanation distinguishing the real milestone (logical-beats-physical error rate) from the categorical gap to useful-scale fault tolerance, citing chapter 6's resource numbers.

lessons.title: NISQ-Era vs. Fault-Tolerant Era: Honest Framing

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself as a direct written rebuttal: someone claims 'fault-tolerant quantum computing has basically already been achieved -- it's just a matter of scaling up what's already been demonstrated.' Using this lesson's NISQ-vs-fault-tolerant framing and chapter 6's resource-estimation math (physical-qubit counts), explain specifically what's wrong or misleading about that claim.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal of the 'already achieved, just needs scaling' claim, citing both the operational NISQ/fault-tolerant distinction and the chapter 6 resource-math gap in orders of magnitude.

lessons.title: Capstone: the Quantum Error Correction Laboratory

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the lesson's own Check Yourself as your capstone deliverable: if the same 50-logical-qubit algorithm instead only needed code distance d=9 (161 physical qubits per logical qubit) because its reliability requirement was looser, compute the new total physical-qubit requirement by hand (50 x 161) and write up how that changes the 'how far from NISQ-era hardware' conclusion compared to the lesson's own d=21 case (44,050 qubits).
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed d=9 total (8,050 physical qubits) for the 50-logical-qubit scenario, plus a written comparison of how much closer (or still how far) this brings the system to current NISQ-era hardware versus the d=21 case.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student understands why real qubits need error correction (decoherence, gate errors, no-cloning), can trace the bit-flip, phase-flip, Shor, and Steane codes by hand using syndrome tables and the stabilizer formalism, understands why the surface code is the leading practical candidate and can compute its real physical-qubit cost at any code distance, and can honestly explain the gap between today's NISQ-era hardware and genuine fault-tolerant computation using the threshold theorem and real resource-estimation arithmetic.
